parsed_answer.content:
In enterprise Java ecosystems, particularly in cloud-native and serverless architectures, JVM startup latency and footprint overhead are critical bottlenecks. AppCDS (Application Class Data Sharing) addresses this performance challenge by extending the classic Class Data Sharing (CDS) mechanism introduced in earlier Java versions. While standard CDS allows standard core library classes from the JDK (like java.lang.Object and rt.jar/modules) to be pre-parsed and memory-mapped into a shared archive file, AppCDS goes a step further by letting developers include application-specific classes, third-party libraries, and framework dependencies into that very same shared archive. This significantly reduces the time the JVM spends on class loading, parsing metadata, and bytecode verification during cold starts.

The mechanics of AppCDS revolve around reducing redundant I/O operations and CPU-intensive metadata parsing. When a JVM starts without CDS, it reads class files from disk or network, parses the raw bytes, performs bytecode verification to ensure type safety, and constructs internal JVM metadata representations (such as InstanceKlass) in native heap memory (metaspace). With AppCDS, this entire workflow is shifted to a training phase. During training, the application runs through a representative workload, and the JVM dumps the resulting memory structures into an archive. In subsequent production runs, the operating system's virtual memory subsystem memory-maps this archive directly into the address space of multiple JVM processes via mmap, enabling Zero-Copy sharing of read-only class metadata across multiple JVM instances.

rows: Reads thousands of individual .class files from disk/JARs
Reads a single contiguous pre-parsed archive via mmap
Performed dynamically at runtime for every loaded class
Pre-verified and serialized directly into the shared archive
High duplication per JVM instance for standard and app classes
Shared across multiple JVM instances via OS-level memory sharing

items: Archive Generation Phase: Requires a three-step process consisting of dynamic class list recording, archive creation, and application execution using the generated archive.
Memory-Mapped Sharing: The shared archive uses OS-level virtual memory mapping, allowing multiple JVM processes on the same host to share read-only class metadata pages in physical RAM.

Class Path Consistency: The classpath used during the archive generation phase must strictly match the classpath used during production execution; otherwise, the JVM falls back to standard loading or throws errors.

parsed_answer.content:
# Step 1: Unlock commercial features and create a class list during a training run
java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app-cds.jsa -cp my-app.jar com.example.Main

# Step 2: Validate and generate the shared archive
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app-cds.jsa -XX:SharedClassListFile=class-list.lst -cp my-app.jar

# Step 3: Run the application using the generated AppCDS archive for rapid startup
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app-cds.jsa -cp my-app.jar com.example.Main

A common production gotcha with AppCDS is classpath drift. If your deployment pipeline injects a different version of a JAR file or alters the classpath order between the archive generation phase and the runtime phase, the JVM will detect a checksum mismatch. Depending on configuration flags, it will either throw an invalid CDS file error or silently fall back to slow standard class loading, masking the regression and leaving you wondering why your startup times haven't improved.
